subject: Agriculture
title: The First Sheep and Goats
description: One-minute skill: The First Sheep and Goats.

hook.text: Sheep and goats were among the first animals domesticated—about 10,000 years ago in the Fertile Crescent.

buildup.text: Wild sheep (mouflon) and bezoar goats were small, docile enough to manage, and ate almost anything.

discovery.text: Early herders selected for tameness. Over generations, animals lost aggression and developed woolly coats.

twist.text: Wild sheep have hair, not wool. The thick fleece we know was bred—it doesn't exist in nature.

climax.text: Sheep and goats spread with humans across every continent except Antarctica, adapting to every climate.

punchline.text: We made wool. Nature only made hair.

quiz.question: Where were sheep and goats first domesticated?

details.summary: Sheep and goats were among the first animals domesticated for food, fiber, and milk in the Fertile Crescent around 9,000–11,000 years ago. This topic covers their wild ancestors, how domestication changed their biology, and why they remain critical to global agriculture.
details.whyItMatters: Sheep and goats thrive in marginal environments where cattle cannot, making them essential livestock for billions of people in arid and mountainous regions worldwide.
takeaways: Goats were domesticated from the bezoar ibex around 10,000 years ago in western Iran
Sheep descend from the Asiatic mouflon, domesticated for meat before wool was selected
Together, sheep and goats number over 2 billion worldwide today

faq.question: Which was domesticated first, sheep or goats?
faq.answer: Goats were likely domesticated slightly before sheep, around 10,000 years ago from the bezoar ibex in the Zagros Mountains. Sheep followed from the Asiatic mouflon, initially kept for meat and milk before woolly varieties were selected.

faq.question: Why are sheep and goats important for smallholder farmers?
faq.answer: They are affordable, require less feed and water than cattle, tolerate harsh environments, reproduce quickly, and provide meat, milk, fiber, and skins. For millions of subsistence farmers, they are the primary livestock and economic asset.
